articles.title: He spent a year on ‘Mars’: NASA science officer emerges from mock mission
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 09 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03588-wEngineer Matthew Montgomery, who has just finished a 378-day simulated Mars mission, talks about what it was like to be out of contact with the rest of humanity for a two-week blackout.
articles.content:
Matthew Montgomery, the science officer of a simulated Mars mission organized by NASA, takes part in a ‘Martian’ geology project.Credit: NASA

Could you survive a year on Mars?

Four engineers now have a well-informed take on the answer. On 31 October, the four emerged from a 158-square-metre, 3D-printed habitat at NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston, Texas, after spending just more than a year inside it for a simulated mission on the red planet.

The exercise was the second in a series of extended NASA simulations that aim to test how long-duration space missions affect astronauts’ health and performance. For more than a year, the crew members grew their own crops, conducted science experiments and performed ‘Marswalks’ on a model of the planet’s surface outside their habitat.

Can you terraform Mars?

The mission also replicated the communication delays that astronauts on Mars would experience when contacting Earth: messages from the crew to mission control and vice versa took 13–22 minutes to arrive, varying with the distance between Earth and Mars. The crew even dealt with a planned two-week communication blackout, with no access to mission control or the outside world, similar to what Martian astronauts would face when the Sun blocks transmission of radio signals between Mars and Earth.

The lessons learnt from these simulations will help NASA to understand how isolation and limited resources affect astronauts’ well-being and productivity, the agency says. NASA will use the results to inform protocols for crewed missions to Mars, which it has said could happen as soon as the early 2030s, as well as future trips to the Moon.

Nature spoke to Matthew Montgomery, a hardware-engineering design consultant and co-owner of a film-production company, who served as the mission’s science officer, to learn about his year on ‘Mars’.

What were your responsibilities as the mission’s science officer?

Prior to the mission, I had worked in controlled-environment agriculture and studied factors such as the best LED lighting for crop growth, so I led the growing of our crops in the simulation. I’ve grown leafy greens, peppers and tomatoes outside of the mission in large growth facilities, and we were growing some of those same crops in the mission. It was also fun to grow those plants — just interacting with Earth-based things like plant life has a cognitive benefit as well as a nutrient benefit.

Matthew Montgomery displays vegetables grown in the hydroponic garden inside the simulated Martian habitat. Credit: NASA

Geology was another huge portion of the mission. Rock collection is going to be incredibly important in a real mission to Mars, so we tried to mirror some of those aspects in the simulation. We analysed rock samples, performed mineral identification and simulated core analysis that Martian astronauts would do to study the geologic history of Mars.

How did the crew get along in such close quarters?

The crew spent a lot of time together prior to the mission, so we got to work on our teamwork and build relationships. We went on a winter camping expedition in Wyoming, where we encountered a blizzard! These high-pressure scenarios set a nice foundation for pre-training, where we spent five weeks together before going into isolation. Through all of those tools that we built, we had a really good dynamic as a team inside of the habitat, and conflict was very minimal.

What was the two-week communication blackout like?

We spent about a month preparing for the blackout. We were communicating with the ground teams to make sure we had all the procedures, schedules and goals for the two weeks. We put safety plans in place to make sure we had reviewed the right protocols if something went wrong.
articles.reasoning: The article reports on a successful, year-long NASA simulated Mars mission that provides valuable insights into astronaut health, teamwork, and operational challenges for future crewed Mars missions. This has broad significance for space exploration and humanity's potential to reach Mars, with detailed context on the mission's scientific and psychological aspects.

articles.title: Newest Sample, Oldest Rock?
articles.summary: Written by Tasha Coelho, Mastcam-Z Student Collaborator at Arizona State University Nov. 1, 2026 Perseverance’s most recent abrasion “Pumbe” bears a striking resemblance to an earlier abrasion, “Badger Peak.” That’s no coincidence. As previously reported, that rock had a hardness too high to core. However, the team felt strongly that it was worth the effort […]
articles.content:
NASA’s Mars Perseverance rover acquired this image of the rock sample “Singita” inside the rover’s coring bit using its left Mastcam-Z camera. The image was acquired on Oct. 24, 2026 (Sol 2018), at a local mean solar time of 12:56:57, shortly after the coring operation. NASA/JPL-Caltech/ASU

Written by Tasha Coelho, Mastcam-Z Student Collaborator at Arizona State University

Nov. 1, 2026

Perseverance’s most recent abrasion “Pumbe” bears a striking resemblance to an earlier abrasion, “Badger Peak.” That’s no coincidence. As previously reported, that rock had a hardness too high to core. However, the team felt strongly that it was worth the effort to add a gabbro, an igneous rock made mostly of calcium-rich plagioclase feldspar and pyroxene crystals, to Perseverance’s sample collection. In search of a new local gabbroic candidate to sample, Perseverance traveled about 100 meters (330 feet) to a different patch of light-toned rocks. Indeed, visual and chemical data from the light-toned rocks in the new workspace revealed a composition similar to that of “Badger Peak.”

NASA’s Mars Perseverance rover acquired this image of the abrasion patch “Pumbe” using its SHERLOC WATSON camera, located on the turret at the end of the rover’s robotic arm. The image was acquired on Oct. 17, 2026 (Sol 2011), at a local mean solar time of 16:14:35. The abrasion patch is about 5 centimeters (2 inches) across. NASA/JPL-Caltech

To improve the odds of collecting a sample this time, the team made prudent decisions: choosing a neighboring rock with a flatter surface better oriented for the drill stabilizers to press against, and using a coring bit with less wear. At last, in a display of the rover’s namesake quality, the drill made it about 3.1 centimeters (1.2 inches) into the rock. Sample acquisition activities followed, making “Singita” the rover’s first sample in more than a year. While Singita is the newest sample, it may be among the oldest rocks in Perseverance’s collection. Textures in the rock suggest that it likely formed deep in the crust and was modified and excavated by at least one, and possibly multiple, large impact events.

Perseverance has now completed its 66th successful abrasion and collected an intriguing new sample alongside it. The latest mission status report opens with “Perseverance remains healthy and stable on Mars” and lists “Spacecraft Status: Nominal.” Translation: the rover remains capable of continued fruitful exploration, with many more abrasions to come.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a significant achievement by NASA's Perseverance rover in successfully collecting a valuable rock sample on Mars, which may be among the oldest in its collection. This represents a meaningful scientific breakthrough with broad implications for planetary science and understanding Mars' geological history. The story is focused, detailed, and highlights ongoing exploration capabilities, making it inspiring and hopeful for space exploration.
articles.personality_title: NASA’s Perseverance rover collects oldest Mars rock sample yet
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – NASA’s Perseverance rover has been exploring Mars to study its rocks and collect samples. Some rocks are too hard to drill into, making it challenging to gather important pieces for study back on Earth.

**What happened** – On October 24, 2026, Perseverance successfully drilled into a rock called “Singita,” collecting a sample after more than a year without a new one. This rock is similar to a previously studied but too-hard rock named “Badger Peak.” The team chose “Singita” because it had a flatter surface and used a fresher drill bit, allowing the rover to drill about 3.1 centimeters deep.

**Impact** – The “Singita” rock may be one of the oldest samples Perseverance has gathered. It likely formed deep inside Mars’ crust and was changed by big impacts over time. This helps scientists learn more about Mars’ early history and the events that shaped its surface.

**What’s next step** – Perseverance remains healthy and ready to keep exploring. Scientists expect it to continue making new abrasions and collecting more samples, which will deepen our understanding of Mars.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Perseverance’s new rock sample, possibly one of the oldest on Mars, marks a key step in uncovering the planet’s geological past.

articles.title: How neutrinos are beginning to reveal the secrets of our galaxy
articles.summary: Columnist Chanda Prescod-Weinstein says understanding neutrinos is one of the most pressing scientific issues in physics. She shares the latest neutrino discoveries that are exciting her and that could bring us new insights about the galactic centre
articles.content:
Columnist Chanda Prescod-Weinstein says understanding neutrinos is one of the most pressing scientific issues in physics. She shares the latest neutrino discoveries that are exciting her and that could bring us new insights about the galactic centre

Artist’s composition of the Milky Way seen through a neutrino lens (blue) Credit: IceCube Collaboration/U.S. National Science Foundation (Lily Le & Shawn Johnson)/ESO (S. Brunier)

The day before this year’s Nobel prize in physics was announced, I was quoted in The New York Times as saying the question of why neutrinos are non-trinary is one of the most pressing scientific issues facing my field. What a happy coincidence that the next day, the Nobel committee announced the prize had been given to Francis Halzen for his leadership on the IceCube Neutrino Observatory. I joked on social media that I was somehow responsible for the committee noticing this important experiment in Antarctica, which studies neutrinos that come from deep space, often looking for how they provide information that other signals – light, gravitational waves – cannot by themselves.

Regular readers of this column know that I love to talk about these subatomic particles because they have the distinct property of being non-trinary. There are three flavours of neutrino and, as they travel through space, they oscillate between these identities. Neutrinos refuse the notion of a fixed identity. We understand these oscillations to be related to their mass. But we actually still don’t understand how they get their mass.

Despite this mystery, we do know plenty about where neutrinos are made. One place is in stars, including our own sun. The nuclear fusion processes that make all the light we get from stars also make neutrinos as a by-product. Those same phenomena also play a role in stellar deaths, like the fantastical explosions we call supernovae. In fact, next year we will be celebrating the 40th anniversary of our first time connecting observed neutrinos with such an explosion.

Advertisement

The first supernova detected in 1987 – designated Supernova 1987A – was a brilliant collapse of a former blue supergiant star. It was the closest supernova to our solar system in centuries, and we witnessed it across the electromagnetic spectrum: optical, infrared, ultraviolet and even in the X-ray. But one of the most interesting things about 1987A’s discovery is that hours before the light became visible, three different neutrino detectors on Earth noticed an influx of these ghostly particles.

In other words, neutrinos were our first messenger from the stellar death that occurred 168,000 light years away. The reason the neutrinos arrived first is down to how deeply antisocial they are. Neutrinos pass by other matter like it’s not even there. So, while the light particles – made in stars alongside neutrinos – were trying to escape the plasmas and atoms they ran into, the neutrinos were streaming freely out of the collapsing star into the cosmos.

In the 39 years since 1987A’s neutrinos helped us place bounds on the mass of neutrinos, and also how many neutrino flavours there are, neutrino astrophysics has become a new vista on the universe.

The IceCube Neutrino Observatory research facility at the South Pole in Antarctica Sven Lidstrom, IceCube/NSF

In the years after 1987A, Halzen led the group that conceptualised IceCube to use those neutrinos as a lens on the cosmos. Over the past few decades, thousands of scientists have worked together to make this concept into a reality in Antarctica and used the instrument to do some truly fascinating science. For example, Naoko Kurahashi Neilson at Drexel University in Pennsylvania led the effort to make a complete map of the Milky Way using only neutrinos. It took almost a decade, but, in 2023, IceCube unveiled a groundbreaking new atlas of our home galaxy. The image is very different from what we get with light: it’s not symmetric and is full of neutrino blobs that are begging us to figure them out. The asymmetry is especially tantalising to me because that’s usually an indicator that something interesting is happening – but what?

These days, Neilson is leading a group within IceCube that is trying to understand what neutrinos can tell us about the galactic centre, especially any details about what is accelerating particles in the region to relativistic speeds. In September, the group shared new research about the challenges of matching neutrino sources with the most high-energy light sources we know, on the assumption that the neutrinos and the light are coming from the same place. The hope is that we can establish what exactly is sending these energetic and mysterious particles out into the void. From my point of view, they’re showing that our galaxy is one of the best naturally occurring particle physics experiments out there.
articles.reasoning: The article highlights significant scientific progress in neutrino astrophysics, including the Nobel-winning IceCube Neutrino Observatory's groundbreaking mapping of the Milky Way using neutrinos. This research offers new insights into the galaxy's center and particle acceleration, representing a major breakthrough in understanding fundamental physics and the cosmos with broad scientific and societal impact.
articles.personality_title: How neutrinos are unlocking new secrets of the Milky Way
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Neutrinos are tiny particles that come from stars and other places in space. Scientists have been trying to understand them better because they behave in unusual ways and carry important information about the universe.

**What happened** – A big discovery was made by the IceCube Neutrino Observatory in Antarctica, led by scientist Francis Halzen, who won a Nobel Prize for this work. IceCube has created the first detailed map of our galaxy, the Milky Way, using neutrinos instead of light. This map shows strange patterns and clusters that could help explain what’s happening at the center of our galaxy.

**Impact** – This is a new way to study space because neutrinos pass through matter almost without being stopped, unlike light. They arrive from places that are hard to see with normal telescopes. The IceCube map reveals unusual features in the Milky Way that scientists think are clues about how particles get sped up to very high energies. This helps us learn more about the galaxy’s center and the forces at work there.

**What's next step** – Researchers are now working to match the neutrino signals with other types of signals like high-energy light. They want to find the exact sources of these particles and better understand the processes that send them across space. This could lead to new discoveries about how the galaxy works and the nature of particle physics.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Scientists are using neutrinos to create a new view of the Milky Way, revealing hidden details about our galaxy’s center and the powerful forces within it.

articles.title: NASA’s Chandra Finds Source of Star’s Mysterious Outbursts
articles.summary: Using NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory, astronomers have discovered what is triggering repeated outbursts from a giant, unstable star. A new study, published Monday in the latest issue of The Astrophysical Journal, details the discovery of a previously hidden companion object that keeps pulling material away from the massive star every 113 days as they orbit […]
articles.content:
A composite NASA Chandra X-ray and Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) optical image of the galaxy NGC 4559 located about 30 million light-years from Earth. The Chandra data shows X-ray point sources represented in purple, and the SDSS data shows the galaxy and foreground and background objects in red and blue. The luminous blue variable and supernova impostor AT 2016blu is in the middle of the small square. X-ray: NASA/CXC/Univ. of Virgina/M. Aghakhanloo et al.; Optical: SDSS; Image Processing: NASA/CXC/SAO/P. Edmonds

Using NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory, astronomers have discovered what is triggering repeated outbursts from a giant, unstable star.

A new study, published Monday in the latest issue of The Astrophysical Journal, details the discovery of a previously hidden companion object that keeps pulling material away from the massive star every 113 days as they orbit one another. This partner is either a stellar-mass black hole, or the dense collapsed core of a massive star called a neutron star.

This is the first X-ray detection of one of this class of erupting stars. It is also the first of these objects found with a black hole or neutron star companion.

The volatile star, known as AT 2016blu, is in the spiral galaxy NGC 4559, located about 30 million light-years from Earth. Astronomers estimate the mass of this star is at least 33 times that of the Sun.

“For 15 years, astronomers have been watching this star get really bright and then dim again on a regular basis,” said Mojgan Aghakhanloo of the University of Virginia in Charlottesville, who led this study. “Until we were able to get Chandra data at the right time, we couldn’t figure out what was making this happen.”

The star AT 2016blu is a type of luminous blue variable, which are hot, massive stars characterized by changes in brightness. Eta Carinae, for example, is a particularly well-known luminous blue variable.) AT 2016blu is a special type of luminous blue variable that undergoes rapid and repeated increases in brightness. The spikes in brightness are so extreme that they resemble supernova explosions, where a massive star collapses onto itself and material then hurtles outward into space. However, unlike in a supernova explosion, the star is not destroyed, so AT 2016blu is also referred to as a “supernova impostor.”

Between 2012 and 2026, astronomers detected at least 27 bursts of optical light, or light in wavelengths that are visible to our eyes, from AT 2016blu roughly every 113 days.

“This star’s behavior was confusing at first because it kept acting like a supernova, but clearly it’s not because it keeps surviving these outbursts about three times a year,” said co-author Núria Torres-Albà, also of the University of Virginia. “To understand the cause of these eruptions, we realized we needed X-ray data, timed so that we’d observe the star when it was in an outburst.”

The team used Chandra because it is the only X-ray telescope with sharp enough vision to distinguish AT 2016blu from another nearby bright X-ray source.

Images showing AT 2016blu in outburst and quiescence. The top-left image shows optical data obtained March 14, 2026, by the Katzman Automatic Imaging Telescope (KAIT), when AT 2016blu was in quiescence, or not in outburst, and the top-right image shows KAIT data from March 25, 2026, when the source was in outburst. The bottom-left image shows NASA’s Chandra X-ray data obtained in 2001 and 2002, before AT 2016blu’s first observed outburst in 2012, and the bottom-right image shows Chandra data obtained between March 24 and March 27, 2026. X-ray: NASA/CXC/Univ. of Virgina/M. Aghakhanloo et al; Optical: NSF/KAIT

“We suspected that the bright repeating flashes at optical wavelengths might actually be powered by periodic blasts of high-energy X-rays,” said co-author Nathan Smith of the University of Arizona in Tucson. “The dense gas surrounding the system is heated by the X-rays and then glows in the optical. So, we needed to plan the Chandra X-ray observations carefully to be simultaneous with an optical outburst.”

Chandra data from March 2026 revealed that AT 2016blu was at least 100 times brighter in X-rays than in Chandra data from 2001 to 2002, which is before the outbursts began. The best explanation for this is that material from the star is falling onto a neutron star or black hole during the closest approach in their oval-shaped orbit around one another. When they come close together, material ejected by the star gets captured by the black hole or neutron star. The material orbits at very high speeds close to the speed of light, getting so hot that it shines brightly in X-rays.

AT 2016blu is bright enough in X-rays to be classified as a candidate of ultra-luminous X-ray source. These are rare, bright X-ray sources found with telescopes like Chandra that astronomers have yet to fully understand. Scientists’ current thinking is that some of them contain neutron stars, and others have black holes.

These new observations suggest there could be a link between ultra-luminous X-ray sources and the kind of violent stellar eruptions seen in AT 2016blu, especially because many ultra-luminous X-ray sources undergo large changes in X-ray brightness.

The discovery of this system may also help studies of stars that change in brightness before they undergo supernova explosions. Astronomers suspect that much of this behavior may be caused by systems containing a massive star orbiting a compact object or another massive star.

To collect the optical data, the team used the Katzman Automatic Imaging Telescope, the Las Cumbres Observatory Global Supernova Project , and observations from the American Association of Variable Star Observers, including those from more than 30 amateur astronomers, to monitor the star’s brightness.

When these observations showed that the star was in outburst in early 2026, Chandra observations were triggered and obtained in March 2026 as part of its “Target of Opportunity” program designed to take account of special events.

NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama, manages the Chandra program. The Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory's Chandra X-ray Center controls science operations from Cambridge, Massachusetts, and flight operations from Burlington, Massachusetts.

To learn more about Chandra, visit:

https://nasa.gov/chandra

Visual Description

This release features a composite image of a spiral galaxy with a giant, unstable star at its outer edge. Using Chandra, astronomers have discovered the star's previously hidden companion, which triggers luminous outbursts every 113 days.

The spiral galaxy is NGC 4559. Shown at a sharp angle in the composite image, its flat pink and milky blue face tilts toward our upper left. Sitting near the outer edge of the dense spiral, near the center of the frame, is a small group of pink and blue dots. This group is outlined with a white square, enlarged and annotated in supporting images.

The smallest pink dot in the square is AT 2016blu, a massive star some 33 times the size of our Sun. For over 15 years astronomers have been watching this star get bright and then dim again in optical light on a regular basis. Chandra's X-ray observations suggest that a hidden companion object, either a stellar mass black hole or a neutron star, is pulling material from AT 2016blu every 113 days as they orbit one another. This captured material gets so hot that it shines brightly in X-rays.

Other pink and blue specks within the white square and enlargement are unresolved stars or star clusters, too distant to be related to the movement of material between AT 2016blu and its hidden but influential neighbor.

articles.personality_title: NASA’s Chandra reveals hidden companion causing star’s repeated outbursts
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – For over 15 years, astronomers have observed a giant star named AT 2016blu in a galaxy 30 million light-years away. This star regularly brightens and dims in a pattern that puzzled scientists because the bursts looked like supernova explosions but the star did not explode.

**What happened** – Using NASA’s Chandra X-ray Observatory, a team led by Mojgan Aghakhanloo discovered that AT 2016blu has a hidden companion—a black hole or neutron star—that orbits the star every 113 days. This companion pulls gas from the star, which heats up and shines brightly in X-rays, causing the star’s repeated outbursts.

**Impact** – This is the first time X-rays have been detected from this type of erupting star, and the first time such a companion has been found. It helps scientists understand how some stars can survive violent outbursts and links these events to ultra-luminous X-ray sources, a mysterious class of bright X-ray objects.

**What's next step** – Astronomers will continue monitoring AT 2016blu and similar stars to learn more about how stars behave before they explode as supernovae. This discovery also encourages further study of how black holes and neutron stars affect nearby stars.

**One-sentence takeaway** – NASA’s Chandra found a hidden black hole or neutron star companion that causes a massive star’s repeated bright outbursts by pulling material from it every 113 days.
articles.personality_title_fr: Chandra de la NASA révèle un compagnon caché à l’origine des explosions répétées d’une étoile
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Depuis plus de 15 ans, les astronomes observent une étoile géante nommée AT 2016blu située dans une galaxie à 30 millions d’années-lumière. Cette étoile s’éclaire et s’assombrit régulièrement, un phénomène qui intriguait car ces éclats ressemblaient à des supernovas, mais l’étoile ne disparaissait pas.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Grâce à l’observatoire à rayons X Chandra de la NASA, une équipe dirigée par Mojgan Aghakhanloo a découvert qu’AT 2016blu possède un compagnon caché — un trou noir ou une étoile à neutrons — qui orbite autour de l’étoile tous les 113 jours. Ce compagnon attire du gaz de l’étoile, qui chauffe et émet des rayons X, provoquant ainsi les explosions répétées.

**Impact** – C’est la première détection de rayons X pour ce type d’étoile en éruption, et la première fois qu’un tel compagnon est trouvé. Cela aide les scientifiques à comprendre comment certaines étoiles survivent à des explosions violentes et établit un lien avec les sources ultra-lumineuses de rayons X, un type mystérieux d’objets très brillants.

**Prochaine étape** – Les astronomes vont continuer à surveiller AT 2016blu et d’autres étoiles similaires pour mieux comprendre le comportement des étoiles avant qu’elles n’explosent en supernova. Cette découverte encourage aussi l’étude de l’influence des trous noirs et étoiles à neutrons sur leurs étoiles voisines.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Chandra de la NASA a découvert un compagnon caché, trou noir ou étoile à neutrons, qui provoque les éclats répétés d’une étoile massive en lui arrachant du matériau tous les 113 jours.
articles.personality_title_es: Chandra de la NASA descubre compañero oculto que causa las explosiones repetidas de una estrella
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Durante más de 15 años, los astrónomos han observado una estrella gigante llamada AT 2016blu en una galaxia a 30 millones de años luz. Esta estrella se ilumina y se apaga en un patrón que confundía a los científicos porque las explosiones parecían supernovas, pero la estrella no explotaba.

**Qué pasó** – Usando el Observatorio de rayos X Chandra de la NASA, un equipo liderado por Mojgan Aghakhanloo descubrió que AT 2016blu tiene un compañero oculto, un agujero negro o una estrella de neutrones, que orbita la estrella cada 113 días. Este compañero atrae gas de la estrella, que se calienta y brilla en rayos X, causando las explosiones repetidas.

**Impacto** – Es la primera vez que se detectan rayos X de este tipo de estrella eruptiva y la primera vez que se encuentra un compañero así. Esto ayuda a los científicos a entender cómo algunas estrellas sobreviven a explosiones violentas y conecta estos eventos con las fuentes ultraluminosas de rayos X, un grupo misterioso de objetos muy brillantes.

**Próximo paso** – Los astrónomos seguirán observando AT 2016blu y estrellas similares para aprender más sobre el comportamiento de las estrellas antes de explotar como supernovas. Este hallazgo también impulsa el estudio de cómo los agujeros negros y estrellas de neutrones afectan a las estrellas cercanas.

**Conclusión en una frase** – Chandra de la NASA encontró un compañero oculto, un agujero negro o estrella de neutrones, que provoca las explosiones brillantes y repetidas de una estrella masiva al atraer material cada 113 días.
